Small pure-UI items may share one Pull Request. ### SPEC-AMEND — A spec that contradicts a rule is amended, and the rule is never weakened to fit it. - **Applies to:** any conflict between a spec and a standard - **Checked by:** review - **Bad:** a Section that keeps an old flag as an alias, which NLG forbids - **Good:** the Section amended to drop the alias - **Why:** a spec is one instance, while rules are the constants every spec shares. ## Grounding and mechanism ### SPEC-RULES — Applicable Rules names the exact rule identifiers the diff will trip, from standards this repository has. - **Applies to:** the Applicable Rules section - **Checked by:** review - **Bad:** "Follow the code rules." - **Good:** "`tests.md`: TCF, TEST-PARTIAL; `languages/rust.md`: ERR-RS" - **Why:** named identifiers give the implementer exact rules to check, while a generic pointer earns review findings. ### SPEC-READ — Each read-first item starts with an existing repository path or an `https://` URL, and files the spec creates belong in Files Changed. - **Applies to:** the read-first list - **Checked by:** review - **Bad:** "1. `src/new_module.rs` — mirror this" for a file that does not exist yet - **Good:** "1. `crates/api/tests/project_grants.rs` — the route test to mirror" - **Why:** a pointer that does not resolve sends the implementer to guess. A correctness-critical requirement is stated in the spec as well as cited, because a reader given only the spec cannot open the link. ### SPEC-PRIOR — Prior Art names a reference implementation to mirror, or says greenfield and points at the architecture page that defines the shape. - **Applies to:** the Prior-Art section - **Checked by:** review - **Bad:** a new command designed with no reference and no reason - **Good:** "Reference: the nearest existing handler and the HTTP standard; divergence: none" - **Why:** mirroring a known-good shape avoids reinventing a solved pattern. Command-line work states which of six practices it follows: - command, handler and error layers kept apart; - handlers that neither print nor exit; - one rendering layer; - structured JSON errors with suggestion and retry fields; - tests at the handler, in-process and subprocess tiers; - JSON by default when stdout is not a terminal. ### SPEC-FILES — Files Changed lists every file the work creates, edits or deletes, by role, never by line number or function name. - **Applies to:** the Files Changed table - **Checked by:** review - **Bad:** "`api.rs` lines 40–80"; a fixture the change edits but the table omits - **Good:** "`tests/support/project.rs` | EDIT | seeds the new column" - **Why:** the table scopes review and orphan sweeps, and line numbers drift. The table includes the spec itself, its move to `done/`, the changelog entry and any architecture page. It also names real writers and readers, schema registration, grants, fixtures, deployment and secret references, and protocol docs. Edits outside it need the owner's approval. ### SPEC-BLAST — A teardown, rename or flip spec lists every word-boundary hit of its token across the repository, with production and test files apart. - **Applies to:** specs that delete, rename or flip a name, flag or path - **Checked by:** review - **Bad:** `grep -rn '"old_name"' src/`, a quoted literal behind a path filter - **Good:** `git grep -n -w old_name` from the root, with every hit in Files Changed - **Why:** YAML and multiline strings carry no quotes, and a path filter misses same-directory references. The spec's invariant and rubric searches use the same pattern as this discovery search. Hits that share the spelling but not the meaning are listed apart. ### SPEC-GREP — A zero-match search gate names product phrases, never a common English word. - **Applies to:** rubric rows and invariants that assert a pattern matches nothing - **Checked by:** review - **Bad:** `\b(run)\b` must match nothing - **Good:** `run interrupt|spec init|gate loop` must match nothing - **Why:** a gate that fires on ordinary English forces contorted prose. ### SPEC-MECH — A pinned mechanism names its state authority, guarded transition, commit-before-release boundary and failover assumption. - **Applies to:** Sections and Invariants that promise safety, uniqueness or single use - **Checked by:** review - **Bad:** "Preserve single use." - **Good:** "The `used_at` column is the authority; `UPDATE … WHERE used_at IS NULL` claims the token; the claim commits before the response." - **Why:** an implementer can obey a vague sentence and still break the invariant. A bounded prototype may leave a performance parameter open; an unchosen security mitigation is not ready to build. ### SPEC-PIN — A pinned detail records its source revision and the proofs that rerun when it changes, and a client-server claim is verified on both sides. - **Applies to:** versions, identity scope, uniqueness, privilege boundaries, release order, failure behaviour and resource budgets - **Checked by:** review - **Bad:** "the client follows cluster redirects" with no version named - **Good:** the client version from `Cargo.lock`, the datastore server version, and the failover test to rerun when either changes - **Why:** an unpinned compatibility claim breaks silently on the next upgrade. ### SPEC-PROSE — A spec states mechanisms and proofs in prose and points at code to mirror, with no code listings, variable lists, line-by-line schema statements or test code. - **Applies to:** Section bodies - **Checked by:** review - **Bad:** a 60-line function inside §2; a `CREATE TABLE` listing every column - **Good:** "Pin identity, null and deletion semantics and grants; mirror the nearest migration; Dimension 2.1 proves it." - **Why:** listings go stale and invite copying, while a mechanism and its proof stay true. Interface examples, evidence commands and referenced diagnostics are allowed. ### SPEC-ORDER — Section prerequisites form an acyclic order, and release or migration order is pinned when correctness depends on it. - **Applies to:** Section dependencies and the Depends on header - **Checked by:** review - **Bad:** §2 needs §4's table while §4 needs §2's API - **Good:** "§1 migration, then §2 API, then §3 CLI; the migration deploys before the API" - **Why:** a cycle has no first slice to build. ### SPEC-DECIDE — Agent defaults, measured outputs and human decisions are recorded apart, and human acceptance is a `manual` proof with its procedure and evidence. - **Applies to:** Sections, Dimensions and Discovery - **Checked by:** review - **Bad:** "Indy accepted the risk" with no quote; an agent marking a manual check passed - **Good:** "Implementation default: a per-project lock, because …"; a `manual` Dimension naming the person, the steps and where the evidence lands - **Why:** an invented sign-off is scope the owner never accepted. ### SPEC-IFACE — The Interfaces section locks every surface other code depends on, and changing one amends the spec first. - **Applies to:** HTTP endpoints, request and response shapes, and shared signatures - **Checked by:** review - **Bad:** renaming a response field during implementation with the spec unchanged - **Good:** amend Interfaces, then change the code and its tests - **Why:** callers and tests are written against the spec's shapes. ### SPEC-INVARIANT — Every invariant is enforced by code: the compiler, a linter, a compile-time assertion or a runtime check. - **Applies to:** the Invariants section - **Checked by:** review - **Bad:** "Reviewers make sure no handler logs a token." - **Good:** "The `Secret` type implements no `Display`, so logging it does not compile." - **Why:** review discipline fails on the first busy day. An operator procedure is a prerequisite, not a runtime guard. Each invariant names its authority, its mechanism and its failure assumptions, and its test is the shortest counterexample. ## Proof ### SPEC-DIM — Every Dimension names one test, its tier and the concrete input and expected output that test asserts. - **Applies to:** Dimension lines - **Checked by:** review - **Bad:** `- **Dimension 2.1** — handles errors` with no test named - **Good:** `` - **Dimension 2.1** — expired tokens are refused → Test `should_reject_expired_token` (unit): an hour-old token returns 401 `` - **Why:** a Dimension without a test is not implemented. Each tier names what its test reaches: - `unit`: logic and boundaries; - `integration`: the real stack, with deterministic injection; - `e2e`: the real path of a user-facing Category (SPEC-E2E); - `manual`: human acceptance, with its procedure and evidence (SPEC-DECIDE). Each promised result names a plausible false pass its check rejects. ### SPEC-TESTS — A Dimension is `DONE` only when the test it names exists in a tracked test source and passes. - **Applies to:** marking a Dimension `DONE` - **Checked by:** review - **Bad:** marking 2.1 `DONE` after lint passes; a test name that appears only in the spec - **Good:** `should_reject_expired_token` passes in the Section's lane, and `DONE —` lands in the same commit as the code - **Why:** a name in the spec proves only that someone typed it. Formatting and lint never mark a Dimension `DONE`. A Dimension of tier `manual` carries durable evidence in place of a test source. ### SPEC-WIRED — A Dimension is `DONE` only when a production entry point calls the code it delivers. - **Applies to:** marking a Dimension `DONE` - **Checked by:** review - **Bad:** a tested `refresh_quota()` that no handler calls - **Good:** the route handler calls `refresh_quota()`, and a test reaches it through the route - **Why:** tested code that nothing calls ships nothing. ### SPEC-FAIL — Every Failure Mode and error row has a negative test, and at least half the Dimensions prove failure paths. - **Applies to:** Failure Modes, error tables and Dimensions - **Checked by:** review - **Bad:** a "dependency unavailable" Failure Mode with an empty Test cell - **Good:** `should_503_when_cache_down` in both the Failure Mode row and a Dimension - **Why:** a failure path without a test is a promise nobody checks. Failure Modes cover timeout, malformed input, auth failure, network blip, race, replay, exceeded quota and dependency unavailable where they apply. A timeout is told apart from a rollback, and an acknowledgement from durable recovery. Partial setup or delivery states what is kept, what resumes it, and how a retry avoids a duplicate effect. A known limit with no mitigation needs an owner disposition in Discovery. ### SPEC-E2E — A spec with a user-facing Category carries at least one end-to-end scenario through the real path. - **Applies to:** specs whose Categories include CLI, UI or API - **Checked by:** review - **Bad:** unit tests alone for a new command - **Good:** a subprocess test that runs the built command-line binary against a live daemon - **Why:** each unit can pass while the wired path fails. ### SPEC-METRICS — Metrics & Observability declares each product or operator event with its test, or states that no signal changed. - **Applies to:** the Metrics & Observability section - **Checked by:** review - **Bad:** an empty table; an event first found in review - **Good:** `project_created` with its allowed properties, privacy guard and test; or "N/A: no product or operator signal changes." - **Why:** a missing event is an implementation gap that ships unseen. Event properties never carry raw email, passwords, tokens, one-time passwords or key material. A changed funnel updates the repository's analytics playbook in the same Pull Request. ## Rubric, deferral and transfer ### SPEC-RUBRIC — The Acceptance Rubric holds 5 to 12 outcome rows, each with a copy-paste Verify command and a mechanically checkable Expected value. - **Applies to:** the Acceptance Rubric - **Checked by:** review - **Bad:** one row per Dimension; Expected "works correctly"; a Verify command containing a pipe - **Good:** `R2 | Expired tokens are refused (§2) | make test-unit-all | exit 0 | P0` - **Why:** one scoring surface with checkable rows makes grading mechanical. S rows carry every declared `conform` and `verify.*` command verbatim, plus `gitleaks detect --redact --no-banner`. A pipeline is wrapped in a script, because a Markdown table escapes the pipe character. ### SPEC-GRADE — Each Graded cell holds ✅ or ❌ and one decisive output line from running its Verify command verbatim. - **Applies to:** the Graded column at VERIFY and at close - **Checked by:** review - **Bad:** ✅ with no output; a pasted wall of log; an empty cell at close - **Good:** `✅ test result: ok. 1412 passed; 0 failed` - **Why:** missing evidence counts as ❌. S rows point at the final `orly gate pr` run recorded in the Pull Request Session Notes. ### SPEC-SHIP — A ❌ row ships only as its priority allows: P0 never, P1 with an owner quote naming it, P2 and P3 with a Discovery disposition. - **Applies to:** closing a spec and opening its Pull Request - **Checked by:** review - **Bad:** a P0 row at ❌ with "follow-up" written in Discovery - **Good:** every P0 row ✅ or `MOVED`; a P2 ❌ with its cause and next step in Discovery - **Why:** a failing P0 row is the spec's core promise broken. A disposition that defers work is a deferral and needs the owner quote too. ### SPEC-MOVE — A `MOVED to M_ R` row names a successor that carries the criterion as its own P0 row, with the mapping in both specs and the owner's quote in Discovery. - **Applies to:** transferring a rubric criterion to another spec - **Checked by:** review - **Bad:** `MOVED to M41_002` where M41_002 has no matching row - **Good:** both specs map each moved Dimension, and Discovery quotes the owner authorising the transfer - **Why:** a one-sided transfer is a deferral under a new name. A `MOVED` row is never ✅: the criterion is still unmet, and the rubric names its new owner. ### SPEC-DEFER — A spec item is deferred only when Discovery quotes the owner naming it, and until then it stays in scope and blocks close. - **Applies to:** Sections, Dimensions and rubric rows described as deferred - **Checked by:** review - **Bad:** "Dimension 2.3 deferred to a follow-up", written by the agent - **Good:** `> Owner (, ): "" — context: ` under Discovery's deferrals bullet - **Why:** an agent-written deferral is incomplete scope, not a decision. PR-DEFER in the pull request standard holds the same rule for claims made in a Pull Request. ### SPEC-MODEL — A model review is advice, and Discovery records its model, version, finding counts and dispositions, never its raw output. - **Applies to:** EGM reviews and any other model review of a spec or diff - **Checked by:** review - **Bad:** a pasted review transcript; "the model approved it" cited as proof - **Good:** "EGM review, : 7 findings, 6 fixed, 1 declined with its reason" - **Why:** a model score proves neither completion nor delivery. Repository content goes to an outside model only with the owner's approval, with secrets and private data removed.

# Tests

This standard covers test names, what a test must prove, how live-dependency tests stay real and isolated, and what a verification claim carries. A coding agent reads it before writing or changing a test; a reviewer reads it to judge a diff's tests. Proof rules for spec Dimensions live in [the spec standard](spec.md).

## Naming

### TST-NAM — Test filenames and test names carry no milestone, workstream, Section or Dimension identifier.
- **Applies to:** test files and test functions in every language
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `m24_001_cross_workspace_idor.rs`; `it("M28_001 3.3: Jira valid signature")`
- **Good:** `cross_workspace_idor.rs`; `it("should accept a valid Jira signature")`
- **Why:** a milestone closes within a cycle, while the test lives as long as the code it covers.

### TNM — A test name states the behaviour it verifies, and a test file is named for the subject it covers.
- **Applies to:** test functions and test files in every language
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `it("does not retry — wait, it retries once")`; `tests/metering_m18.rs`
- **Good:** `it("should retry once on a 502")`; `tests/metering_telemetry.rs`, named for the flow it proves
- **Why:** a failing test's name is the first thing an engineer reads, and a narrated or dated name sends them hunting.

Unit tests sit beside the code they cover; an integration test file names the flow, endpoint or invariant it proves.
Comments in tests follow NRC and CODE-MSID in the code standard.

## What a test proves

### TCF — A test fails when the clause, guard or branch it covers is deleted.
- **Applies to:** every new or changed test
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a tenant-scope test that asserts only absence and still passes with the scope clause deleted; a check asserting only an exit code
- **Good:** delete the clause, see the test fail, restore it; assert what the check found, such as the count, symbol or line
- **Why:** a vacuous pass and a real pass look identical from outside, so the suite stays green after the guarantee is gone.

A test that survives removal of its own subject is repaired or deleted, never kept for coverage.

### TEST-MUTATE — A red run mutates a value inside the function under test and fails at an assertion.
- **Applies to:** proving that a new or changed test can fail
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** deleting the call to `scope_filter()` to see red, which leaves the helper unused and fails the build instead
- **Good:** flip `>=` to `>` inside `within_quota()`, or run `cargo mutants --in-diff <patch>`, and watch an assertion fail
- **Why:** a build failure shows that the code changed, not that the test checks the behaviour.

### TEST-REDGREEN — A fix's regression test fails on the parent commit and passes on the fix.
- **Applies to:** every change that fixes a bug, incident or regression
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a regression test written beside the fix and only ever run green
- **Good:** run it in `git worktree add ../pre HEAD~1` and see it fail, then pass on HEAD; record both results in the Session Notes
- **Why:** a test that passes on the buggy code does not pin the bug.

### TEST-OUTCOME — A test asserts the outcome: the return value and every side effect the code promises.
- **Applies to:** unit and integration tests
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `expect(sendMail).toHaveBeenCalled()` alone; an integration test asserting only the response body
- **Good:** assert the stored row, the emitted event's fields and the response together
- **Why:** a mock-call or body-only assertion passes while the write is lost.

Log assertions read structured fields from a capturing logger, never a string match.

### TEST-ERROR — A failure test asserts the error's type, code and structured fields.
- **Applies to:** tests of error paths in Rust and TypeScript
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `assert!(result.is_err())`; `expect(run).toThrow()`; `assert!(res.status().is_client_error())`
- **Good:** `assert_eq!(res.status(), 422)` plus the problem body's `code`; `expect(run).toThrow(LimitError)` plus its fields
- **Why:** a bare failure assertion also passes on the wrong failure.

### TEST-NEG — At least half of a changed surface's tests exercise failure paths, including empty, null, maximum, malformed and non-ASCII input.
- **Applies to:** the tests a diff adds for a changed function, handler or command
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** three happy-path tests for a parser
- **Good:** one success case plus empty, oversized, truncated, `\r\n` and emoji input, each asserting its error
- **Why:** bugs live on the paths a happy case never walks.

### TEST-PUBLIC — A test drives the public surface and states expected values literally.
- **Applies to:** unit tests
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `assert_eq!(total(&items), items.iter().map(|i| i.price).sum())`; a helper made `pub(crate)` only for a test
- **Good:** `assert_eq!(total(&items), 4_200)` over a fixture whose prices are known
- **Why:** a test that re-implements the function agrees with its bugs, and one that reaches past the surface breaks on every refactor.

A private function that needs its own tests is public in practice, so it is promoted.

### TEST-REACH — An uncovered branch is first shown reachable from a fixture, then tested through the verb that composes it.
- **Applies to:** tests added to cover a changed branch
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a unit test calling the leaf `parse_suffix()` with input no caller can produce
- **Good:** build the fixture that reaches the branch through `project create`, then assert through that command
- **Why:** a branch no input reaches is dead code to delete, and a leaf test misses how the verb composes it.

### TVR — Test values are values the schema and types allow, unless the test asserts their rejection.
- **Applies to:** fixtures and inputs for code behind a schema or typed boundary
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** inserting `0` into a column declared `CHECK (size_bytes >= 512)` and asserting success
- **Good:** 512 accepted and 511 rejected by the real constraint
- **Why:** an unreachable value passes in isolation and fails at integration.

A drift test compares against an independent statement of the schema; comparing code with itself catches nothing.

### TEST-TRUTH — When code and spec disagree, the test asserts the spec and the code is reported as the defect.
- **Applies to:** writing or changing an expected value
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** editing the expected value until it matches what the code returns
- **Good:** keep the spec's value, let the test fail, then fix the code or raise the conflict
- **Why:** a test bent to the code proves only that the code does what it does.

Observed runtime behaviour, such as logs and incidents, outranks the spec; a conflict between them is raised before testing.

### TEST-DIFF — Every changed public function, new branch and new error path in a diff has a test or a recorded reason it has none.
- **Applies to:** every code-changing diff
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a new `match` arm with no test and no note
- **Good:** the arm's test, or `needs-infra: Linux sandbox only` recorded in the Session Notes
- **Why:** a bare gap is a defect, not a deferral.

### TEST-BRANCH — Coverage means branch coverage: each clause of a condition, each early return and each error path gets its own input.
- **Applies to:** tests for conditions, normalisers and guards
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** one `"y"` input covering `s === "" || s === "y" || s === "yes"`
- **Good:** inputs for empty, `"y"`, `"yes"`, `"no"`, upper case and padded text
- **Why:** line coverage marks the whole condition covered after one input.

Coverage gates read the aggregate. Lines the compiler erases, such as `import type`, are never chased per file or hidden with ignore entries.

### TEST-GOLDEN — A snapshot or golden file changes only with a written reason, and never stands as a test's only assertion.
- **Applies to:** snapshot tests and golden output files
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** rerunning with `-u` to accept a changed snapshot; a test whose only check is `toMatchSnapshot()`
- **Good:** the commit names the behaviour that changed the output, and a behavioural assertion sits beside the snapshot
- **Why:** a silently accepted snapshot records the bug as the expected output.

### TEST-DRY — Tests favour explicit setup, and a shared helper exists only when three or more tests share setup that hides no logic.
- **Applies to:** test helpers and shared setup
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a `build_world(flags)` helper whose branches decide what each test gets
- **Good:** each test builds the two rows it needs, and one helper seeds the project every test shares
- **Why:** logic inside a helper hides what an assertion depends on.

## Fixtures and data

### TFX — Test fixtures use the production constants, never copies of their values.
- **Applies to:** fixtures, seeds and expected values in tests
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `const DOMAIN = "agentmail.dev"` in a test while production reads `MAIL_DOMAIN`
- **Good:** `import { MAIL_DOMAIN } from "../config"` in the test
- **Why:** three copies of one value drift apart, and only one matches production.

### STL — A test stops writing a wire field in the same change that removes the field from the parser.
- **Applies to:** test request bodies and builders after a wire-protocol field is removed
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** keeping `"stage_id": 1` in a test body because the handler now ignores it
- **Good:** remove the field from every test body in the same commit, and delete a test that existed only for that field
- **Why:** a test that sends an ignored field passes while exercising less than its name claims.

### ITF — An integration test seeds the real schema through shared fixture helpers and asserts against the real table.
- **Applies to:** integration tests that touch a production table
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `CREATE TEMP TABLE workspaces (...)` shadowing the real table
- **Good:** a fixture module named for its scope, such as `tests/support/workspace_credit.rs`, with `seed` and an idempotent `cleanup` around each test
- **Why:** a temporary-table mock keeps the old columns and hides the new `NOT NULL` column the real query hits.

Fixture constants and cleanup helpers live in test code, never in production modules. A probe table with no production counterpart is fine.

### TEST-GITENV — A test that runs Git in a scratch repository strips inherited `GIT_*` variables.
- **Applies to:** tests and test helpers that spawn `git`
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a bare `Command::new("git")` in a test that runs under a commit hook
- **Good:** `Command::new("git").env_remove("GIT_DIR").env_remove("GIT_INDEX_FILE").env_remove("GIT_WORK_TREE")`
- **Why:** Git exports variables such as `GIT_INDEX_FILE` to hooks, and a test that inherits them can act on the real repository.

## Live dependencies

### TEST-REAL — An integration test runs real Postgres, the real key-value store, and the real router with its middleware.
- **Applies to:** tests in the integration lane
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** calling the handler function directly with a stub pool
- **Good:** send the request through the router to a migrated Postgres and the local key-value store
- **Why:** integration bugs live in the seams, and a stub removes the seam.

A test that mocks any of these, or an internal module, is a unit test and is labelled one.

### TEST-MOCK — Tests mock only system boundaries: network, disk, external services, clock and randomness.
- **Applies to:** unit and integration tests
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `mock.module("../services/billing", ...)`; a fake repository behind an integration test
- **Good:** a local HTTP server standing in for the payment provider; a fake clock
- **Why:** mocking an internal module tests the fake, and the integration bug ships.

External services are faked at their HTTP boundary, never at the SDK call site.

### TEST-LOCAL — Integration tests run against local containers, never a deployed environment.
- **Applies to:** the integration lane
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a test that calls `https://api.staging.example.com`
- **Good:** the Postgres and key-value store containers the integration lane starts and resets
- **Why:** a deployed target ties results to someone else's data and releases, and the test can damage them.

### TEST-SWITCH — A live-dependency test runs only in a documented lane that CI calls, and never passes silently without its dependency.
- **Applies to:** tests that need Postgres, a key-value store or another live service
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a test that returns early and passes when `DATABASE_URL` is unset
- **Good:** `#[ignore = "needs live Postgres: the integration lane"]`, run by that lane in CI
- **Why:** a silent skip reads as a pass, and nobody learns the lane exists.

### STR — A streaming test proves bytes arrive incrementally at the transport, not only that the parser handles a full buffer.
- **Applies to:** Server-Sent Events (SSE), chunked, WebSocket and other streaming paths
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** feeding a pre-buffered SSE body to the parser
- **Good:** read the first event from the live response while the producer holds the rest, then release the next
- **Why:** a correct parser cannot show whether the HTTP layer buffers the whole response.

Reconnection with `Last-Event-ID`, a slow consumer and a client disconnect each get a test too.

## Failure injection

### TEST-INJECT — Every failure mode named in code or spec has a test that injects it deterministically.
- **Applies to:** error branches, retries and named failure modes
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** "handles connection reset" with no injection mechanism
- **Good:** `pg_terminate_backend(pid)` from a sibling connection mid-transaction; a fake clock past the lease deadline
- **Why:** a failure the test cannot reproduce on demand is fiction.

A timeout and a connection reset are shown to take different paths.

### TEST-PARTIAL — An operation that touches several systems, or acquires one resource twice, has a failure test at each ordered interaction.
- **Applies to:** handlers and services with more than one dependency call
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** draining the connection pool and calling it coverage of every acquisition
- **Good:** a failpoint that fails acquisition 2 of 2, selected by workflow and boundary-call ordinals and scoped to one operation
- **Why:** a drained pool proves only the first acquisition.

The failpoint resets per test, counts safely under concurrency and asserts it fired exactly once. Release, then an external call, then reacquire is the riskiest window.

### TEST-RESIDUAL — A failure-injection test asserts the residual state: durable rows, external effects, the user's next read and the retry outcome.
- **Applies to:** every injected failure
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** asserting only the 503
- **Good:** assert the 503, no orphan row, no remote charge, and a retry that completes exactly once
- **Why:** the response alone hides a half-finished operation.

### TEST-ACKLOSS — Each external mutation has a test where the remote effect commits, its reply is lost, and a retry yields exactly one effect.
- **Applies to:** calls that change state in an external service
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** treating a durable intent row as proof that a retry cannot reissue the remote call
- **Good:** a mock server that commits, then drops the response; the test reads remote state and asserts one effect after retry
- **Why:** a lost acknowledgement turns a naive retry into a second charge.

A mutation that can complete before any durable intent or repair record exists is a design defect to report. Read-only prerequisites are exempt.

### TEST-KILL — A process that holds a lease is tested by `SIGKILL` mid-lease: the lease is reclaimed, the work runs once, and the late report is refused.
- **Applies to:** client daemons such as a job runner, and any process that holds a lease
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** only a graceful `SIGTERM` drain test
- **Good:** `kill -9` the runner mid-lease; assert reclaim with a higher fencing token, one processed event and a stale-token rejection
- **Why:** sudden death is the case a happy-path loop never reaches.

A restart re-registers without duplicate work. A forked child is reaped, and its sandbox removed, on every exit path.

## Isolation and determinism

### TEST-ORDER — Each test resets the state it touches and passes in any order.
- **Applies to:** every test suite
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** test B reads the row test A created
- **Good:** unique identifiers or per-test rollback, proven with `bun test --randomize` or another shuffled run
- **Why:** an order-dependent pass hides coupling that fails once the order changes.

A suite-level reset makes the first run clean; it does not isolate tests from each other within one run.

### TEST-SCOPE — Concurrent live tests isolate on every scope the code reads or cancels: owner, tenant and project.
- **Applies to:** integration tests that run in parallel against shared datastores
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** two tests sharing one tenant, where one test's cancel-all stops the other's runs
- **Good:** each test mints its own owner, tenant and project
- **Why:** a shared scope turns one test's cleanup into another test's failure.

### TEST-RACE — A flaky test is fixed at its race and measured alone and beside its siblings, never by a wider timeout or a clean rerun.
- **Applies to:** any test that fails intermittently
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** raising a wait from 5 to 30 seconds; accepting a green rerun
- **Good:** mint the rows the test scans, wait for the full user-visible end state, then repeat it alone and with its siblings
- **Why:** a wider timeout or a lucky rerun hides the race until production meets it.

### TEST-PORT — A test harness binds its listener once and hands the bound socket to the server.
- **Applies to:** test servers and harnesses that listen on a port
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** ask the OS for a free port, close it, then let the server bind that number
- **Good:** `TcpListener::bind("127.0.0.1:0")` passed straight to `axum::serve(listener, app)`
- **Why:** another test takes the port in the gap, and the server fails with `EADDRINUSE`.

A harness that must reserve a number retries on conflict and never panics on a bind race.

### TEST-TEARDOWN — Test reset derives what it drops from the live catalog or the migration set, never from a hand-kept list.
- **Applies to:** test database reset and teardown code
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a teardown that drops a fixed list of schemas
- **Good:** drop every schema `information_schema.schemata` lists outside the system set
- **Why:** a migration that adds a schema survives a fixed list, and the next run cannot start.

### TEST-COUNTER — Performance and complexity claims are proven with counters, and wall-clock time only as a median of runs against a pinned baseline.
- **Applies to:** performance budgets, N+1 query checks and complexity claims
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `assert!(elapsed < Duration::from_millis(200))` on one sample
- **Good:** count database round trips at n and 10n, and assert linear growth
- **Why:** a counter gives the same verdict on every machine, while one timing sample flakes.

A missed budget is a design finding, and the threshold never loosens silently.

### TEST-CONTEND — An exactly-once or idempotency claim is proven by at least 100 callers released together from a barrier.
- **Applies to:** idempotency keys, leases and concurrent writes to one row
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** two sequential calls with the same key
- **Good:** 100 tasks on one `tokio::sync::Barrier` sharing a key, asserting one row and a peak in-flight count above one
- **Why:** sequential calls cannot reveal a lost update or a hidden global lock.

### TEST-LEAK — A suite that drives live dependencies ends with the open connections, file descriptors and memory it started with.
- **Applies to:** integration suites and long-running request loops
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** no check, or a check after a single request
- **Good:** drive N requests and assert the pool's open count and the heap high-water mark stay flat
- **Why:** a slow leak shows only as growth across many requests.

## Verification evidence

### TEST-LANE — A package-scoped runner proves a package, and only the declared `verify.*` commands prove the repository.
- **Applies to:** any claim that a branch is verified or ready
- **Checked by:** gate: cmd.verify.unit, cmd.verify.integration
- **Bad:** `cargo test -p app_wire` passes, and the message says the tests pass
- **Good:** the commands `.orly/orly.json` declares, such as `verify.unit` and `verify.integration`
- **Why:** a package run skips every other crate and the TypeScript coverage gates.

`orly gate pr` runs every declared command itself and never infers success from a push.

### TEST-CLAIM — A claim that tests pass names the command it ran and the counts it printed.
- **Applies to:** done messages, Pull Request descriptions and Session Notes
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** "Tests pass."
- **Good:** "`make test-unit`: 1,412 passed, 0 failed, 37 ignored."
- **Why:** a bare claim cannot be checked or compared with the baseline.

### TEST-SKIP — A lane that could not run is reported as not run with its reason, never folded into a pass.
- **Applies to:** verification reports
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** "Tests pass" while Docker was down and the integration lane never started
- **Good:** "`verify.integration` not run: Docker unavailable; unit lane passed with the counts above."
- **Why:** a hidden skip reads as proof.

### TEST-EXIT — A verdict is the command's own logged exit status, never a pipeline's last stage, a trailing `echo`, a background notice or `| tail`.
- **Applies to:** agents and scripts that judge a command's result
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `make X 2>&1 | tail -2 && git commit`
- **Good:** `make X > log 2>&1; echo "EXIT=$?" >> log`
- **Why:** `tail` exits 0 whatever the command did, so the commit proceeds on a failure.

The zsh shell has no `PIPESTATUS` array, and `sh -c 'false | tail -1; echo $?'` prints 0.

### MKP — A Make recipe never pipes a command whose status matters into a filter unless the recipe shell sets `pipefail`.
- **Applies to:** `Makefile` and `make/*.mk` recipes
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `@cargo test 2>&1 | tail -3`
- **Good:** drop the pipe, or set `SHELL := bash` and `.SHELLFLAGS := -eu -o pipefail -c`
- **Why:** Make's `/bin/sh` reports the pipeline's last status, so the recipe passes while the test fails.

### TEST-ABSENT — An absence claim counts only when the same check finds a known positive and fails loudly on error.
- **Applies to:** empty searches, zero counts and "pre-existing" claims
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `.unwrap_or(0)` turning a failed count query into "zero rows"; an empty search over a mistyped path
- **Good:** `.expect("count tenant rows")`; the same search run first on a file known to match
- **Why:** a check that cannot find anything reports absence for free.

### TEST-DELTA — A diff that adds code adds tests: the unit count rises over the recorded baseline, or the Pull Request says why not.
- **Applies to:** code-adding branches before the Pull Request opens
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a new handler, an unchanged unit count and no note
- **Good:** baseline and branch counts from the same lanes in the Session Notes, with each removed test explained
- **Why:** a flat count on new code means the code shipped untested.

# Architecture

This standard covers the names, cardinality and flows that a repository's `docs/architecture/` owns, and how a decision about them lands. It applies to code, specs, design conversations and answers about how data moves between components.

## Grounding

### ARCH-GROUND — Every architectural name, cardinality claim and flow description matches the `docs/architecture/` topic file that owns it.
- **Applies to:** names for streams, channels, key-value store namespaces, consumer groups, queues, remote procedure call (RPC) methods, Postgres schemas and tables
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `A spec names a new stream run_events when the topic file already calls it project_runs.`
- **Good:** `The spec uses project_runs and cites the topic file's section.`
- **Why:** Names and flows recalled from memory drift away from the system that ships.

Claims such as one consumer per stream, flow descriptions, answers about data flow and proposals to change any of them are covered too.
Each topic is checked against its own file, and a read for one topic does not cover the next.

### ARCH-WINS — Where a spec or code disagrees with `docs/architecture/`, the doc wins until the owner reconciles the two.
- **Applies to:** specs, implementation and reviews that touch an owned name, cardinality or flow
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `Code follows a spec's new cardinality while the topic file still says one consumer per stream.`
- **Good:** `The conflict is raised with the section it contradicts, and the change waits for the owner.`
- **Why:** Specs are instances, and the architecture doc is the constant they all follow.

## Landing

### ARCH-LAND — An architecture decision reaches `docs/architecture/` in a doc-only commit before its code, or in the same commit, and never after it.
- **Applies to:** new names, cardinality, flows and invariants, including greenfield designs and decisions the doc was silent on
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `A punch-list task to capture the architecture after the slice lands.`
- **Good:** `A doc-only commit on the branch now, or the doc edit inside the code commit.`
- **Why:** A doc that trails its code misleads every reader in between.

### ARCH-CHAT — A design settled in conversation that names a channel, asserts cardinality, traces a flow or defines an invariant is an architecture decision under ARCH-LAND.
- **Applies to:** design discussions in chat, before any code exists
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `A chat design kept only in a task note for after the code ships.`
- **Good:** `A doc-only commit before the next agent action, or an owner-approved deferral into the code commit.`
- **Why:** A design held only in chat is lost to the next agent.

A picked-up task that defers the capture until after its code is rewritten to land the doc first or with the code.

## Both homes

### ARCH-HOMES — A branch that changes flow-defining code changes `docs/architecture/`, or its pull request notes say why nothing architectural changed.
- **Applies to:** branches that touch flow-defining code
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `A branch that adds a queue and leaves docs/architecture/ untouched, with no note.`
- **Good:** `The branch diff carries the queue's topic-file edit.`
- **Why:** Internal design truth drifts silently when code moves without it.

### ARCH-PUBLISHED — A change to documented user-facing behavior revises the affected published pages, and a changelog entry alone does not count.
- **Applies to:** changes to endpoints, the command-line interface (CLI), flags and flows users see
- **Checked by:** gate: docs.updated
- **Bad:** `A new flag ships with a changelog entry and no reference-page edit.`
- **Good:** `The flag's reference page changes in the same release, in the repository that owns it.`
- **Why:** When internal docs and published pages diverge, users and maintainers believe different systems.

The gate sees only this repository's declared docs paths, so review covers a docs repository kept elsewhere.
A docs repository outside this checkout is edited on its own branch, with its owner's approval.
Internal-only reshaping needs no published edit, and the pull request notes say so.

# Authentication, authorization and secrets

Rules for who may reach an endpoint, how secrets are stored, shown and compared, and how signed or single-use proofs are checked. A coding agent applies them before touching guards, tokens, credentials or auth flows. A reviewer judges a diff against them, and auth is a security boundary with no exceptions beyond those stated here.

## Routes and ownership

### AUTH-DOC — Token lifecycle, session shape, the auth layer chain and credential storage follow the repository's `docs/AUTH.md`.
- **Applies to:** the repository's auth and credential modules, token-minting handlers, credential-typed spec Dimensions
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a new token prefix or session field that `docs/AUTH.md` does not describe
- **Good:** a change that matches the flow `docs/AUTH.md` documents, or updates that document in the same diff
- **Why:** the product's auth document is the one description of every flow, and code that departs from it goes unreviewed.

### AUTH-GUARD — Each route row declares exactly one guard, and the capability a caller needs is the row's scopes.
- **Applies to:** route definition files
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a second authentication check inside a handler, or a webhook route mounted under `Guard::Bearer`
- **Good:** `Guard::Bearer` with `Scopes::rw(PROJECT_READ, PROJECT_WRITE)`, `Guard::RunnerBearer` for runner credentials, and a signature guard for signed deliveries
- **Why:** the router mounts the guard from the row, so a handler never runs for a caller who should not reach it.

The signature guards are `Guard::WebhookHmac`, `Guard::WebhookSignature` and `Guard::Svix`.
In `Scopes::ByMethod { get, otherwise }`, `otherwise` is the more privileged scope, so an unplanned method is refused too often, never too rarely.

### AUTH-OPEN — A `Guard::Open` route states in its module documentation what verifies its caller.
- **Applies to:** routes mounted with `Guard::Open`
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** an open route whose module says nothing about who may call it
- **Good:** a webhook module naming the per-project signature it verifies over the body, under a buffer cap
- **Why:** an open route that verifies nothing and says nothing is a bug, and its proof can only be checked after the body is read.

Only the probes `/healthz` and `/readyz` verify nothing.
Device-flow session routes verify the code itself, connector callbacks a signed `state` parameter, and webhooks a signature.

### WAUTH — Every workspace-scoped operation authenticates the caller and proves workspace ownership before it reads or writes data.
- **Applies to:** workspace routes, their guards and their tests
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** discarding the principal, or relying on an ownership helper that no served route mounts
- **Good:** the row's guard and the template's `{workspace_id}` mount both checks, and tests refuse unauthenticated and wrong-workspace callers on the served route
- **Why:** without the ownership check, any authenticated caller reads another workspace by changing the path.

Handlers neither authenticate nor call an ownership check by hand, because the mounted layers do both.

### AWO — A path naming a workspace and a resource inside it proves the resource belongs to that workspace, and answers `404` when it does not.
- **Applies to:** routes with `{workspace_id}` and a child identifier such as `{project_id}`
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** reading the project by `id` alone once the workspace check passes, or answering `403` on a mismatch
- **Good:** the statement filters `WHERE id = $2 AND workspace_id = $1`, and no row answers `404` with `PROJECT_NOT_FOUND`
- **Why:** the workspace check proves only the caller-to-workspace edge, and a `403` would reveal which identifiers exist elsewhere.

An insecure direct object reference (IDOR) test requests the route with another workspace's project and asserts `404`.

### BIL — Billing and credential endpoints require their dedicated capability, never workspace access alone.
- **Applies to:** routes that expose billing figures or credential material
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a project billing summary mounted with `PROJECT_READ`, so every member who can read projects sees cent totals
- **Good:** `Scope::BillingRead` on billing routes, and `SECRET_READ` or `SECRET_WRITE` on credential routes
- **Why:** workspace ownership says nothing about role, and billing and credential data belong to privileged members only.

A test calls the route as a workspace member without that scope and asserts `403`.

### CTX — Data a sandboxed agent must not read across tenants sits behind a process boundary, never a shared filesystem.
- **Applies to:** storage for memory, caches and per-tenant files that sandboxed agents can reach
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a bind-mounted `/var/lib/agent-memory/{project_id}/` shared by sibling sandboxes and scoped only by path
- **Good:** Postgres behind the scoped `memory_runtime` role
- **Why:** an agent with any shell or file tool reads a sibling's directory and bypasses the scoping the API enforces.

### AUTH-CORS — Cross-Origin Resource Sharing (CORS) is declared per endpoint, and no endpoint allows every origin.
- **Applies to:** endpoints the dashboard calls from a browser, and edge and router configuration
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`
- **Good:** the dashboard origin declared in the spec for the endpoints the browser calls, with cross-origin requests refused at the edge elsewhere
- **Why:** a wildcard lets scripts on any origin call the API from a user's browser.

Public ingress is HTTPS only, enforced at the Cloudflare Tunnel. Adding browser access to an endpoint is a surface change.

## Secrets

### AUTH-SECRET — A secret-shaped response field is write-only or one-time-read, and its OpenAPI schema says which.
- **Applies to:** response fields whose names contain `token`, `secret`, `key`, `password` or `credential`
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `GET /v1/api-keys/{key_id}` returning the raw key
- **Good:** the raw key only in the create response, marked `x-secret-handling: one-time-read`
- **Why:** a secret readable on every `GET` spreads into caches, logs and screenshots.

A name that only identifies a secret, such as `key_name`, is not secret-shaped.

### AUTH-NOLOG — A resolved credential never reaches command output, a transcript, the event log or an agent's context.
- **Applies to:** code and tooling that loads secrets, and agent sessions that handle them
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** pasting the output of `op read 'op://…'`, or a provider token written into a project event
- **Good:** `op read` at runtime into the process that needs it, and the secret substituted at the tool bridge inside the sandbox
- **Why:** a printed secret lands in transcripts and backups that outlive its rotation.

Log records follow LOG-SECRET in [logging.md](logging.md).

### AUTH-LOGID — A log call at `INFO` or above never carries a raw workspace, project or user identifier.
- **Applies to:** log calls in `**/*.rs` and `**/*.ts`
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `tracing::info!(workspace_id = %workspace_id, "project created")`
- **Good:** the identifier at `DEBUG`, or a same-line `// log-id-allowed: <reason>` when the value is safe, such as a hashed prefix
- **Why:** identifiers in routine logs let anyone with log access map tenants and their activity.

### AUTH-RANDOM — Identifiers and secrets come from the shared identifier module and the operating system's cryptographic source, never a custom generator.
- **Applies to:** code that mints identifiers, tokens, nonces or keys
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a seeded `SmallRng`, or `Math.random()`, minting a token
- **Good:** `app_core::id` for identifiers, and `app_crypto::entropy` for secret bytes
- **Why:** a predictable generator makes identifiers and secrets guessable.

## Comparisons and proofs

### CTM — Secrets, tokens and signatures are compared in constant time.
- **Applies to:** comparisons of tokens, passwords, nonces, digests and Hash-based Message Authentication Code (HMAC) tags
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `presented == expected` in Rust, `token === stored` in TypeScript
- **Good:** `expected.as_bytes().ct_eq(presented.as_bytes())` from `subtle`, or `timingSafeEqual` from `node:crypto`
- **Why:** a short-circuit comparison leaks, through its timing, how many leading bytes matched.

### CTC — A secret comparison takes the same path whatever the input lengths are.
- **Applies to:** constant-time helpers and their callers
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `if a.len() != b.len() { return false; }` before the comparison loop
- **Good:** compare fixed-length digests such as `HmacSha256Tag`, or loop over the shorter length and fold the length mismatch in after the loop
- **Why:** an early return on length tells the caller how long the expected secret is.

### CTE — A constant-time helper's comment claims only what the helper hides.
- **Applies to:** doc comments on comparison helpers
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** "prevents timing leaks on secret value or length" above a loop over `min(a.len(), b.len())`
- **Good:** "`ct_eq` short-circuits on length, not content; the digest length is public"
- **Why:** a later caller with variable-length input would inherit a guarantee the code does not give.

### TWF — A freshness check rejects a timestamp too far in the future as well as one too far in the past.
- **Applies to:** webhook and signed-request verification
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `now - ts <= MAX_DRIFT` alone, which accepts any timestamp in the future
- **Good:** `ts <= now + MAX_DRIFT && now - ts <= MAX_DRIFT`, with the future bound checked first
- **Why:** an accepted future timestamp lets an attacker pre-sign a request and replay it after the window.

### OAE — An OAuth form body encodes every field value, the authorization code included.
- **Applies to:** OAuth token exchanges and any `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` body
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `format!("grant_type=authorization_code&code={code}&client_id={}", encode(client_id))`
- **Good:** `client.post(url).form(&Grant { … })`, which encodes every field through `serde_urlencoded`
- **Why:** a code containing `+`, `&` or `=` silently corrupts the body and draws a confusing error from the provider.

### GATDL — A single-use token in a key-value store is consumed by one script that compares and deletes atomically.
- **Applies to:** nonces, approval keys, cross-site request forgery (CSRF) tokens and device-flow codes held in a key-value store
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `GETDEL` followed by the comparison, or `GET` and `DEL` sent as two commands
- **Good:** one `EVAL` script that reads `KEYS[1]`, compares it with `ARGV[1]`, deletes the key only on a match, and returns 1 or 0
- **Why:** `GETDEL` lets a forged guess destroy the real token, and two commands let two requests both pass the read.

The script ships inside its crate through `include_str!`, as a `session/verify_consume.lua` file.

# HTTP responses and errors

Rules for what an endpoint returns: wire types, field names, lists, instants, durations, status codes and error bodies. A coding agent applies them while writing a response or a refusal, and a reviewer judges a diff against them. Paths and methods are in [http.md](http.md).

## Bodies and fields

### RAD — A new or changed endpoint meets the HTTP design rules, and its response holds no acknowledgement or two-meaning field.
- **Applies to:** new or changed endpoints, their wire types and their OpenAPI annotations
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a steer response `{"ack": true, "run_steered": true}`
- **Good:** `{"message_queued": true, "execution_active": false}`, with the status code as the acknowledgement
- **Why:** a response shape is the hardest part to change once tests and the OpenAPI document depend on it.

The design rules it names are HTTP-VERB, HTTP-METHOD, HTTP-PATHID, HTTP-FIELD, HTTP-PROBLEM and HTTP-VERSION.

### HTTP-WIRE — A handler returns a wire type through `IntoResponse`, and builds a response by hand only for a Server-Sent Events (SSE) stream.
- **Applies to:** handlers and the wire-type module
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `(StatusCode::OK, Json(json!({"id": id, "name": name})))` spelled inline in a handler
- **Good:** `Ok(Json(ProjectDetailResponse::from(&detail)).into_response())`
- **Why:** the same struct generates the OpenAPI schema, so field names, status and content type cannot drift.

### HTTP-SINGLE — A single-resource response is the resource itself, with no envelope.
- **Applies to:** response wire types
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `{"data": {"id": "…"}}`, `{"project": {…}}`
- **Good:** `{"id": "…", "name": "Support triage", "created_at": "2026-10-17T18:06:49.123Z"}`
- **Why:** an envelope adds a layer every client must unwrap and every Software Development Kit (SDK) must model.

### HTTP-FIELD — A field name is snake_case, ends `_id` for an identifier and `_at` for an instant, and carries its unit.
- **Applies to:** request and response wire types
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `isEnabled`, `items_completed`, `size`, `owner` holding an identifier
- **Good:** `enabled`, `completed_items`, `size_in_bytes`, `owner_user_id`
- **Why:** consistent names let SDK users guess a field without reading its schema.

Booleans have no `is_` prefix, adjectives come before nouns, and collections are plural.
Brand names and reserved words stay out of field names, and a bare `id` names only the resource's own key.

### HTTP-NAMES — No field is named `data`, `payload`, `object`, `response`, `result`, `value`, `info` or `metadata` on its own.
- **Applies to:** request and response wire types
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `{"data": {…}}`, `{"metadata": {…}}`
- **Good:** a domain noun, such as `usage_line` or `schedule`
- **Why:** these names say nothing and make poor SDK accessors.

The finished-operation body of HTTP-LRO keeps its `result` field.

### HTTP-NULL — An optional field with no value is omitted, and `null` means the value was explicitly cleared.
- **Applies to:** request and response wire types
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `"label": null` for a label that was never set
- **Good:** no `label` key until one is set, and `PATCH` with `{"label": null}` clears it so later reads show `null`
- **Why:** SDK users branch on undefined versus `null`, and mixing the two breaks clients silently.

A lifecycle instant not yet reached, such as an unrevoked key's `revoked_at`, is `null` and declared `nullable: true`.

## Lists

### HTTP-LIST — A list response is exactly `{items, total, next_cursor}`.
- **Applies to:** list endpoints and their wire types
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `{"results": […]}`, `{"data": […], "count": 3}`, or `204` for an empty list
- **Good:** `{"items": [], "total": null, "next_cursor": null}` with status `200`
- **Why:** one envelope lets every SDK page through every list the same way.

`items` is always an array, `total` is an integer or `null` when not computed, and `next_cursor` is always present.
Both nullable keys declare `nullable: true`. `GET /v1/tenants/me/workspaces` also returns `tenant_id`, which clients store with the list.

### HTTP-PAGE — Pagination is keyset, `?starting_after=<id>&limit=<int>` in and `next_cursor` out, parsed by the shared paging code.
- **Applies to:** list handlers
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** reading `limit` from the query string by hand, or an offset parameter
- **Good:** the shared `paging::cursor`, `Page::parse` with the route's `Ceiling`, or `Limit::parse`
- **Why:** shared parsing gives every list one default of 50 and one maximum of 100, tested at the served endpoint.

An empty `limit` uses the route default, and `next_cursor` goes back as the next request's `starting_after`.

### HTTP-FILTER — A filter uses one grammar: comma-separated equality, exclusive `_after` and `_before` bounds, and `include` with a documented enum.
- **Applies to:** list query parameters
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `?created_at[gte]=…`, `?include_events=true&include_runs=true`
- **Good:** `?status=active,paused&created_after=2026-10-01T00:00:00Z&include=events,runs`
- **Why:** one grammar across endpoints lets SDKs model every filter the same way.

An endpoint whose time bounds are inclusive says so in the parameter description.

### HTTP-SORT — A list sorts by one key, `sort=field` ascending or `sort=-field` descending, and offers no sparse fieldsets.
- **Applies to:** list query parameters
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `?sort=status,-created_at`, `?fields=id,name`
- **Good:** `?sort=-created_at`
- **Why:** one key maps onto one keyset cursor, and a slimmer payload is a smaller endpoint, not a knob.

### QPC — Sister endpoints accept the same value set for the same filter.
- **Applies to:** query parameters shared across endpoints, their OpenAPI enums and their tests
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** workspace billing accepts `period_days` of 7, 30 or 90 while project billing silently clamps 90 to 30
- **Good:** one shared constant feeds both handlers and both OpenAPI `enum` lists, and each value is tested on both
- **Why:** a generated SDK exposes one enum per parameter, so a divergent value returns wrong data with no error.

An out-of-set value gets the same treatment on both endpoints, either `400` or the same coercion.

### HTTP-BULK — A batch endpoint answers `207 Multi-Status` with one item per input.
- **Applies to:** batch endpoints
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a batch returning `200` with a bespoke `failures` array
- **Good:** `{"items": [{"id": "…", "status": "succeeded"}, {"id": "…", "status": "failed", "error": {…}}]}`
- **Why:** one shape lets clients handle partial failure the same way on every batch.

An item's `status` is `succeeded`, `failed` or `skipped`, and its `error` is the error envelope without `request_id`.
A malformed batch still fails whole with `4xx`.

## Instants and durations

### HTTP-TIME — An instant is a Request for Comments (RFC) 3339 string in Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) ending `Z`, in a field ending `_at`.
- **Applies to:** wire types, query parameters and cursors
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `"created_at": 1760724409123`, or `"created": "2026-10-17 18:06"`
- **Good:** `"created_at": "2026-10-17T18:06:49.123Z"`, held as `jiff::Timestamp` with its standard serialization
- **Why:** one textual form lets every client parse every instant, and an epoch integer hides its unit.

A request may carry any numeric offset, which the server normalizes to UTC.
An invalid or out-of-range instant answers `400` with a field-specific `detail`, and shared validation enforces the range and millisecond precision.

### HTTP-DURATION — A duration is an integer whose field name ends `_ms` or `_seconds`.
- **Applies to:** wire types and query parameters
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `timeout`, `ttl`, `"PT5M"`, `1.5`
- **Good:** `timeout_ms`, or `ttl_seconds` where the system beneath speaks seconds, such as a key-value store `EX` or a JSON Web Token `exp`
- **Why:** the unit in the name is the only unit a reader of the payload can see.

Mixing `_ms` and `_seconds` in one endpoint needs a reason in its OpenAPI description, and `_ms` is the default choice.

## Status codes

### HTTP-STATUS — A status code means what its entry below says, and `409` and `412` stay distinct.
- **Applies to:** handlers and the error registry
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `409` for a stale `If-Match`, `400` for a missing resource, or an invented code
- **Good:** `409` when the resource's state forbids the transition, and `412` when the caller's version is stale
- **Why:** clients branch on the code, and merging two meanings sends them down the wrong retry path.

`200` is a read or update, `201` a create, `202` accepted work and `204` no content.
`400` is a bad shape, `401` unauthenticated, `403` unauthorized, `404` not found, `413` too large, `429` rate limited and `500` internal.

### HTTP-STATEEXT — A `409` body names `current_state`, a `412` body carries the current `etag`, and no other extension exists unless this standard adds it.
- **Applies to:** refusals with status `409` or `412`
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a `409` whose only explanation is `"detail": "conflict"`
- **Good:** `{"status": 409, …, "current_state": "approved"}` when the gate was already approved
- **Why:** the client needs the current state or version to recover without another read.

A reviewed setup mutation also returns an opaque `review_digest` on a stale-review `409`, which grants no authority.

### HTTP-429 — A `429` carries `Retry-After` in whole seconds and the `X-RateLimit-Limit`, `X-RateLimit-Remaining` and `X-RateLimit-Reset` headers.
- **Applies to:** rate-limited endpoints
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a bare `429` with no headers
- **Good:** `Retry-After: 30`, with `X-RateLimit-Reset` in epoch seconds
- **Why:** without them a client can only guess when to retry.

### HTTP-ETAG — A resource two principals can edit returns an `ETag`, and its writes require `If-Match`.
- **Applies to:** `GET`, `PATCH`, `PUT` and `DELETE` handlers of shared mutable resources
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a last-writer-wins `PATCH` on a shared project configuration
- **Good:** `GET` and `PATCH` responses carry `ETag`, and a test shows a stale `If-Match` answered `412` with the current `etag`
- **Why:** optimistic concurrency stops one editor from silently overwriting another.

A resource without realistic concurrent edits may opt out, with the decision in the spec's Failure Modes section.

## Errors

### HTTP-REGISTRY — Every error response is built from a registry code, never assembled by hand.
- **Applies to:** handlers and the error-code registry module
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a hand-built `Problem`, or `(StatusCode::NOT_FOUND, Json(json!({"error": "not found"})))`
- **Good:** `Refusal::coded(PROJECT_NOT_FOUND, DETAIL_NOT_FOUND)`, `Refusal::malformed(DETAIL_WORKSPACE_ID)` or `Refusal::preconditioned(error.code(), error.detail(), current)`
- **Why:** status, title and documentation link come from one entry, so one error never reaches clients with two spellings.

### HTTP-NEWCODE — A new error code enters the registry with its status, title and documentation link, and a test reaches it.
- **Applies to:** the error registry and its family modules
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a new code constant that a handler returns with no registry entry
- **Good:** the family constant, its registry entry, and a test asserting the entry is reachable, listed in the spec's error table
- **Why:** the registry is the one place a client-facing error is defined.

### HTTP-TITLE — A registry title is a noun phrase of two to five words, in sentence case, with no trailing punctuation.
- **Applies to:** error registry titles
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `error: database is currently unavailable.`, `WORKSPACE_NOT_FOUND`, `Something went wrong while processing your request`
- **Good:** `Database unavailable`, `Insufficient role`, `Invalid webhook signature`
- **Why:** a title must be safe to show verbatim in a user interface toast.

### HTTP-DETAIL — An error `detail` is one sentence or fragment of at most 200 characters, written for a developer calling the API.
- **Applies to:** refusal sentences
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a paragraph explaining the storage layer, or a `detail` that interpolates a `workspace_id`
- **Good:** `key_name must be 1-64 chars, alphanumeric + hyphen + underscore`, `Workspace access denied`, `Project name already exists`
- **Why:** `detail` is user-facing text, and each code keeps one shape of sentence.

A placeholder carries only an enumerable safe value, such as a role label or sort option, never an entity value.

### HTTP-LEAK — An error `detail` never contains internals, secrets or entity values.
- **Applies to:** refusal sentences and the refusal renderer
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `duplicate key value violates unique constraint "uq_projects_name"`, `panic at src/project.rs:42`, `Bearer eyJ…`
- **Good:** `Project name already exists`
- **Why:** a leaked table, path or token helps an attacker and teaches clients to parse internals.

Banned: `pg_` names, table and unexposed column names, SQL keywords, source paths, line numbers, stack traces and addresses.
Also banned: `sk_`, `pk_`, `Bearer `, `eyJ`, `op://`, hex runs over 16 characters, identifier values, emails and vault key names.

### HTTP-500 — An internal failure answers the registry's `500`, and only diagnostics name the failed operation.
- **Applies to:** service and datastore error paths in handlers
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `Refusal::coded(INTERNAL, &err.to_string())`, which puts the driver's message into `detail`
- **Good:** `services.project_detail(&context, project_id).await.map_err(Refusal::at(PROJECT_READ))?`
- **Why:** the operation constant identifies the failure in logs and telemetry, and the caller learns nothing internal.

### HTTP-PROBLEM — An error body is an RFC 7807 problem with `type`, `title`, `status`, `detail` and `request_id`.
- **Applies to:** the refusal renderer
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `{"error": "invalid", "message": "bad id"}`
- **Good:** `{"type": "https://docs.example.com/errors/invalid-request", "title": "Invalid request", "status": 400, "detail": "workspace_id must be a valid UUIDv7", "request_id": "req_…"}`
- **Why:** one envelope lets clients and support trace any failure by its `request_id`.

# HTTP surface: OpenAPI, versions and clients

Rules for how the public HTTP surface is documented, tested, changed and retired, and for the command-line client that calls it. A coding agent applies them before changing a public endpoint, field or command, and a reviewer judges a diff against them. Paths are in [http.md](http.md) and responses in [http-responses.md](http-responses.md).

## The OpenAPI document

### HTTP-OPENAPI — The repository's OpenAPI document is generated from the server, regenerated and committed with the code, and never edited by hand.
- **Applies to:** the repository's OpenAPI document, `#[utoipa::path]` annotations and wire types
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a hand edit to the OpenAPI document, or a handler change committed without regenerating it
- **Good:** the repository's regeneration command, then `git diff --exit-code` on the document it writes
- **Why:** the next regeneration reverts a hand edit, and no test compares the committed document with the build.

### HTTP-ANNOTATE — Every served route has an OpenAPI annotation, and every annotation names a mounted route and the refusals its guard guarantees.
- **Applies to:** handlers and each plane's `src/openapi.rs` collector
- **Checked by:** gate: verify.unit
- **Bad:** a mounted handler with no `#[utoipa::path]`, or an annotation that omits the `403` its scope guarantees
- **Good:** `#[cfg_attr(feature = "openapi", utoipa::path(…))]` beside the handler, named in that plane's collector
- **Why:** `test_coverage_gate_rust_source` and `test_documented_codes_match_refusals` refuse the gap and name the route and method.

### HTTP-PROSE — OpenAPI prose is written at its source: the annotation, or the doc comment on the wire type.
- **Applies to:** `#[utoipa::path]` descriptions and wire-type doc comments
- **Checked by:** gate: verify.lint
- **Bad:** maintainer rationale in a `///` comment that utoipa publishes, or a wording fix made in the generated JSON
- **Good:** consumer-facing prose in the annotation or `///` comment, and maintainer rationale in a `//` comment beside it
- **Why:** the documentation checks read the generated document, so the source is the only place a fix lasts.

### HTTP-TAG — Each top-level resource maps to exactly one OpenAPI tag.
- **Applies to:** the `tag` of every `utoipa::path` annotation
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** project operations split across `Projects` and `ProjectEvents`, or one `Workspaces and Projects` tag
- **Good:** `tag = "Projects"` on every project operation, sub-resources included
- **Why:** generators group operations by tag, so one resource stays one client module.

### CIV — An OpenAPI validator follows every `$ref` to its target instead of skipping it.
- **Applies to:** scripts and tests that validate OpenAPI responses
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a check that inspects inline `content` and passes any response written as a `$ref`
- **Good:** a response with no inline `content` has its `$ref` resolved and compared with the expected shared response
- **Why:** a `$ref` to a legacy error shape otherwise passes the validator unseen.

### HTTP-SDK — A new response pattern is one that Software Development Kit (SDK) generators already handle cleanly.
- **Applies to:** wire types and OpenAPI schemas
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a polymorphic response body added without checking generator output
- **Good:** a shape mirrored from an endpoint known to generate cleanly under Stainless, Speakeasy, APIMatic and OpenAPI Generator
- **Why:** a non-standard pattern breaks client generation on the next bundle.

## Versions and change

### HTTP-VERSION — Every endpoint sits under a URI version prefix, `/v1` today, and no header selects a version.
- **Applies to:** route templates
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `X-API-Version: 2026-04-25`, or an unversioned `/projects`
- **Good:** `/v1/workspaces/{workspace_id}/projects`
- **Why:** one versioning scheme keeps routing, documentation and SDKs aligned.

`/v2` arrives only when a breaking change is unavoidable.

### HTTP-BREAK — A change inside `/v1` is additive: no rename, removal, type or unit change, tightened validation or new requirement.
- **Applies to:** wire types, route templates, query parameters and status codes
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** renaming `project_name` to `name`, a lower maximum length, an optional field made required, or a new default `limit`
- **Good:** add `name`, fill both fields, mark `project_name` deprecated, and remove it only in `/v2`
- **Why:** clients the server cannot see rely on every exposed name, including path and query parameter names.

A different status code for an existing failure is breaking.
A new endpoint, optional request field, request enum value or error code is additive, and so is looser validation.

### HTTP-ENUM — A new value in a response enum waits for `/v2` or ships as an `additional_*` companion field.
- **Applies to:** response enums
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** adding `paused` to a response `status` enum inside `/v1` with no note
- **Good:** `status` left frozen, and `additional_status: "paused"` documented in the OpenAPI description
- **Why:** typed SDKs generate exhaustive matches, so a new value breaks compiles or falls through silently.

A new value that ships inside `/v1` anyway is named in the PR description with the consumers that need a release.

### HTTP-STABILITY — Every new response field declares `x-stability` as `stable`, `beta` or `internal`.
- **Applies to:** new response fields
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a new field with no class, which defaults to `stable` and starts the deprecation clock as it ships
- **Good:** `x-stability: beta` on a field whose shape may still change
- **Why:** the class decides whether the deprecation clock binds, and generators strip `internal` fields.

### HTTP-DEPRECATE — A deprecated endpoint or field sends `Deprecation`, `Sunset` and a `Link` to its migration guide for at least 90 days.
- **Applies to:** deprecated endpoints and fields
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** removing a field one release after announcing it
- **Good:** `Deprecation: true`, `Sunset: <RFC 1123 date>`, `Link: <docs-url>; rel="deprecation"`, and `deprecated: true` with a migration hint in OpenAPI
- **Why:** clients need a visible signal and time to move before anything disappears.

Anything an external SDK consumer touches keeps the headers for 180 days.

### EP4 — An intentionally removed endpoint answers `410 Gone` with a named error code.
- **Applies to:** endpoint removal
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a removed route that now answers `404`
- **Good:** the route kept in the table, answering `410` with its registry code after the deprecation window, and a test proving it
- **Why:** `404` reads as a routing fault to monitors and clients, while `410` says the removal is permanent and intended.

A removal follows the repository's deployed clients and deprecation policy, and states the result clients will see.

### HTTP-SURFACE — A Pull Request (PR) that changes the HTTP surface opens its description with a surface diff.
- **Applies to:** PR descriptions for endpoint, path, query or schema changes
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a PR that adds a response field and renames a query parameter with no list of either
- **Good:** a "Surface diff" section listing added, renamed and removed `(method, path)` pairs and schema fields
- **Why:** reviewers then see breaking changes that the code diff buries.

Exposing an existing endpoint to browsers is a surface change too.

## Tests and budgets

### HTTP-TESTS — An endpoint's integration tests cover the happy path and one case for each refusal it can return.
- **Applies to:** handler test suites
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** one happy-path test for a handler with four refusals
- **Good:** a test per refusal, plus the double-`PATCH`, `Idempotency-Key` replay and stale `If-Match` cases where they apply
- **Why:** each refusal is behaviour a client depends on, and an untested one drifts.

### HTTP-PERF — An endpoint meets p95 under 150 ms and p99 under 200 ms, and runs no unbounded query loop.
- **Applies to:** new and changed endpoints
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a one-line "this endpoint is slow" note standing in for a carve-out
- **Good:** a carve-out in the spec naming the endpoint, measured p50, p95 and p99 with the bench command, the load profile and the reason
- **Why:** an unmeasured exception becomes the new baseline.

The carve-out also names the milestone that retires it, or `accepted-permanent` with a justification the owner reviewed.

## Command-line client

### JCL — The command-line interface's `--json` output carries only stable, documented error codes.
- **Applies to:** `cli/src/**`
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** undocumented `AGENT_ERROR` or `IO_ERROR` codes, or usage text returned as the error message
- **Good:** `{"error": {"code": "UNKNOWN_COMMAND", "message": "unknown command 'project-ls'"}}`, with the code from `REJECTION_CODE`
- **Why:** scripts switch on these codes, so an ad-hoc code or a prose message breaks them.

`UNKNOWN_COMMAND` names the unrecognized token.
A second `jsonMode` check on one path carries a comment saying why both exist.

### CLI-HINT — A renamed or removed command leaves no message, hint, comment or changelog line naming its old syntax.
- **Applies to:** `cli/src/**`, error hints and messages, log lines, doc comments and the changelog entry
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** a hint that still says `Run 'acme install <template>'` after the positional form was removed
- **Good:** every hint and message names the new syntax, found by searching for the pattern and reading the sentence around each hit
- **Why:** a user reads a hint when already confused, and a dead command doubles the failure.

Neither lint nor the type checker reads message bodies, and hints often paraphrase the command.

# HTTP paths, methods and routes

Rules for the shape of the HTTP API: resource paths, methods, idempotency, long-running work, route registration and handler signatures. A coding agent applies them before adding or changing an endpoint, and a reviewer judges a diff against them. Responses are in [http-responses.md](http-responses.md), and OpenAPI, versioning and clients in [http-surface.md](http-surface.md).

## Paths

### HTTP-NOUN — A resource path is a plural noun collection, optionally followed by one identifier.
- **Applies to:** route templates in the repository's route definition files
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `/getProjects`, `/createProject`, `/project/{project_id}`
- **Good:** `GET …/projects` for the collection and `GET …/projects/{project_id}` for one project
- **Why:** OpenAPI generators build clean Software Development Kits (SDKs) from this shape.

### HTTP-NEST — A path nests each resource under the resource that owns it.
- **Applies to:** route templates
- **Checked by:** review
- **Bad:** `GET /v1/projects?workspace_id=…`
- **Good:** `GET /v1/workspaces/{workspace_id}/projects`
- **Why:** the nesting states that the project belongs to the workspace, and the ownership layer reads it from the template.
